intro.label: Before Puppy Comes Home
intro.heading: What do you need before bringing home a Keeshond puppy?
intro.html:
Before your Keeshond puppy arrives, the most time-sensitive preparation is getting pet insurance in place before the first vet visit. Epilepsy appears in this breed at a meaningfully higher rate than most breeds — typically emerging between 1 and 5 years — and coverage needs to be in place before any conditions are documented. PDA (Patent Ductus Arteriosus), a congenital heart defect, is detectable at the first puppy exam and requires prompt attention. Have insurance, have the cardiac check, know the epilepsy signs.

Essential Gear Checklist

  • Medium crate (30–36 inch) with divider for growth
  • Soft dog bed or crate mat
  • Stainless steel food and water bowls
  • Flat collar + ID tag (engrave immediately)
    One option: GoTags Personalized Stainless Steel ID Tag on Amazon. An engraved stainless steel ID tag; you pick the shape and the lines of text at checkout. Put a phone number that's actually answered on it, and update the engraving if you move.
  • Harness for walks (easier on the neck than a collar for a dog that may pull)
  • 4–6 ft leash
    One option: Joytale Double-Handle Leash (6 ft) on Amazon. A 6-foot nylon leash with a padded second handle near the clip for close control, plus reflective stitching for dark walks. The 1-inch webbing suits medium and large dogs; it can feel heavy on a young puppy.
  • Undercoat rake — start using from the beginning to build grooming tolerance and manage the puppy coat
    One option: Maxpower Planet Undercoat Rake on Amazon. A dual-sided rake: the 9-tooth side works through tangles and the 17-tooth side thins out loose undercoat in dense double coats. Work in the direction of hair growth and ease off over bony areas.
  • Slicker brush
    One option: Chris Christensen Big G Slicker Brush on Amazon. The Big G has long, angled pins set in a flexible cushioned pad, built for working through double, long and curly coats. Use light strokes; slicker pins can scratch skin if pressed hard.
  • Wide-tooth steel comb
  • Dog-safe shampoo and conditioner
  • High-value training treats
    One option: Blue Buffalo Bits Soft Training Treats, Beef (19 oz) on Amazon. Soft, bite-size training treats with real beef as the first ingredient, small enough for rapid repetitions. Keep treats to about 10% of daily calories.
  • Age-appropriate toys: durable rubber chews, Kongs, puzzle feeders; the breed is intelligent and benefits from mental enrichment from early on
  • Enzymatic cleaner
    One option: Nature's Miracle Dog Stain & Odor Remover (32 oz) on Amazon. An enzymatic stain and odor cleaner that keeps breaking down urine and other organic messes after you apply it. Spot-test on carpet or upholstery first.

Grooming Habit From Day One

Keeshonds accept grooming well when it's normalized early. Start brush sessions immediately — 5 minutes with treats — and build to full brushing sessions over the first weeks. The payoff is significant: a Keeshond that is accustomed to the undercoat rake, to having its paws handled, and to being dried with a dryer is a pleasure to maintain. One that first encounters the full routine at 6 months is a much larger project.

care.label: Health Monitoring Priorities
care.heading: What should the first week with a Keeshond puppy look like?
care.html:
First Vet Visit (Within 48–72 Hours)

  • Full physical exam
  • Cardiac auscultation — required: PDA (Patent Ductus Arteriosus) creates a distinctive murmur detectable by auscultation. Document the cardiac finding at the first visit. If a murmur is present, request referral to a veterinary cardiologist for echocardiogram. PDA corrected surgically in puppyhood has excellent outcomes.
  • Vaccine schedule verification
  • Parasite prevention
  • Microchip if not done by breeder
  • Discuss spay/neuter timing appropriate for a medium breed
  • Confirm pet insurance is in place before this appointment

Epilepsy: Know the Signs, Know When to Act

Idiopathic epilepsy in Keeshonds typically begins between 1 and 5 years of age. It is not detectable before it happens — there are no pre-symptoms. What matters is recognizing a seizure when it occurs and responding correctly.

Signs of a seizure:

  • Loss of consciousness or sudden collapse
  • Involuntary muscle movements — paddling legs, jerking, muscle rigidity
  • Loss of bladder or bowel control during an episode
  • Post-seizure confusion, disorientation, or temporary blindness (the "postictal" phase) lasting minutes to hours
  • Focal seizures are less dramatic: sudden behavioral change, staring into space, fly-biting, or one-sided facial twitching

What to do:

  • Do not put your hands near the dog's mouth during a seizure — you will be bitten reflexively
  • Keep the dog away from stairs or furniture edges where it could fall
  • Time the seizure — note the start and end time
  • Stay calm; your presence is helpful, your panic is not
  • A single brief seizure (under 5 minutes) is not an immediate emergency — note it and call your vet the next day
  • A seizure lasting more than 5 minutes (status epilepticus) or multiple seizures within 24 hours is an emergency — go to a veterinary emergency clinic immediately

After a first seizure, your vet will typically begin by ruling out other causes (toxin exposure, metabolic disease) before diagnosing idiopathic epilepsy. Bring the time-stamped video of the episode if you can capture one — it significantly helps the diagnostic process.

special.label: Separation Anxiety Prevention and Training
special.heading: Building Good Habits With a Social, Velcro Breed
special.html:
Separation Anxiety Prevention

Keeshonds were barge dogs that lived in close quarters with their people — they are wired for constant company. This makes them wonderful family dogs and creates a real risk of separation anxiety when left alone. Prevention is much easier than remediation:

  • Crate train from day one — the crate provides a safe, comfortable space and prevents the destructive behaviors that develop when an anxious dog has the run of the house
  • Practice departures from the first week: step out for 30 seconds, return calmly, step out again. Build duration gradually. The puppy that learns departures end in returns is calmer than one who only experiences long absences
  • Don't make departures or arrivals dramatic — low-key goodbyes and calm greetings reduce the emotional loading of comings and goings
  • Provide enrichment in the crate: frozen Kongs, puzzle feeders, chew toys — mental engagement during alone time helps

Barking Management

Keeshonds are vocal. Alert barking is a genuine breed trait and will not disappear entirely. Managing it means shaping it — the dog can alert to something once, be acknowledged, and be asked to settle. Teaching "quiet" or "enough" as a trained behavior gives you a tool. Ignoring barking or reacting with frustration makes it worse.

Socialization: Use the Window

8–16 weeks is the critical socialization period. Keeshonds are naturally friendly, but socialization still shapes their adult confidence, their response to strangers, and their ability to settle in new environments.

  • Diverse people: tall/short, different ages, uniforms, hats
  • Diverse environments: urban sounds, traffic, different floor types, public spaces
  • Controlled dog interactions in puppy class — crucial for a dog that will live closely with its family's social life
  • Positive exposure to being alone for short periods, building tolerance gradually

Never Shave Rule: Establish It Early

Tell every groomer, pet sitter, and dog-caring person in your network: the Keeshond double coat is never shaved. Print it on the grooming instructions if you board the dog. Groomers who are unfamiliar with double-coated breeds sometimes clip them in summer as a default — preventing this requires explicit communication every time.

faq.q: What is PDA and how serious is it in Keeshond puppies?
faq.a: Patent Ductus Arteriosus is a congenital heart defect where a blood vessel present in the fetus (the ductus arteriosus) fails to close after birth. This forces the heart to work harder and can lead to heart failure if untreated. The good news: when detected early by cardiac auscultation (a murmur is audible) and corrected surgically, outcomes are excellent. The first puppy exam is the opportunity to catch this — make sure your vet listens to the heart and documents the finding.

faq.q: How will I know if my Keeshond develops epilepsy?
faq.a: Epilepsy typically begins between 1 and 5 years, not in puppyhood. The first seizure is usually the first warning. Knowing what a seizure looks like (see the health monitoring section above), keeping your vet informed, and having pet insurance in place from the beginning are the practical preparations. You cannot prevent epilepsy in an affected dog — you can only be prepared to recognize and manage it.

faq.q: How much daily brushing does a Keeshond puppy need?
faq.a: Keeshond puppies have softer, less dense coats than adults, so brushing is less labor-intensive early on. 5–10 minutes of brushing 2–3 times per week is typical for the puppy coat. Use this time to build grooming tolerance — it's more important for habituation than for actual coat management. The adult coat that grows in around 12–18 months requires more work: 15–20 minutes of brushing once or twice a week in normal periods, and daily during coat blows.
